hints: Do not start with a score. Start with what a good meeting summary must get right, and which of those mistakes would hurt a user most.

This is property-based evaluation with layered graders: annotated references, deterministic code checks, a calibrated judge for narrow questions, and human calibration, run over slices with repeated trials.

List the properties (faithfulness, owner accuracy, action-item recall and precision, decisions, no invented dates, empty handling), then design the dataset slices and splits, pick a grader per property, and define the ship gate with counts and denominators.

signals: Breaks quality into named, severity-ranked properties instead of one holistic rating
Builds a versioned dataset with hard slices (no-decision meetings, reversed decisions, reassigned items, same-name attendees, transcription errors) and a held-out split
Uses code checks where possible (attendee names, date phrases, format) and narrow judge questions elsewhere, with judge evidence verified against the transcript
Calibrates the judge against human labels and names biases to watch, such as preferring longer text
Runs repeated trials per transcript and reports per-slice counts with denominators against the current production baseline
Closes the loop with online signals such as user edits and deleted action items feeding new cases
followups: Recall rises from 81% to 88% but unsupported claims rise from 0.5% to 0.9% of claims. Do you ship?
